chunks.text: 2 Method 2.1 Overview As illustrated in Figure 1 -(a), MCDNet first embeds the input CT slice into patches and processes the resulting features through a U-shaped encoder–decoder built from MCSS blocks. Each block combines morphology-aware local enhancement with channel-decoupled long-range modeling. A final class projection produces a segmentation tensor of size H × W × C H\times W\times C , where C C denotes the number of anatomical classes. 2.2 Morphology-Aware Channel-Decoupled State-Space Block The MCSS block couples adaptive local feature extraction with separate state-space processing of channel groups. As shown in Figure 1 -(b), it incorporates an MAEM into each group before SS2D-based spatial modeling, allowing local shape information and long-range context to be modeled within the same processing stream. Given an input feature map X ∈ ℝ H × W × C X\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} , where C C denotes the feature-channel dimension in this block, we first apply LayerNorm and a linear projection, and then split the channels into N N groups. The group count is set to the number of segmentation classes, providing an anatomical basis for the channel decomposition. The resulting groups provide separate feature streams in which differentiated structural representations are learned end to end through segmentation supervision. (1) When C C is not divisible by N N , the remaining channels are assigned to the last group. The channel partition is fixed, while the feature transformations and fusion weights are learned. Each group is first refined by an MAEM to adapt its local responses to morphological variation, and then independently processed by an SS2D unit to capture long-range spatial dependencies.

Stacking MCSS blocks in the encoder–decoder connects morphology-aware local enhancement with channel-decoupled long-range modeling throughout MCDNet.

2.3 Morphology-Aware Enhancement Module To explicitly model local morphological variation, we introduce an MAEM within each channel group. Organs vary in shape, scale, and boundary geometry, making a fixed sampling pattern potentially insufficient for their local representation. MAEM predicts deformable convolutional offsets from the input features to adapt sampling locations to local image structure. Depthwise–pointwise convolutions then refine the sampled responses, and channel attention selectively weights the resulting features. These operations are combined within a residual framework to preserve the input representation. Finally, a residual connection adds the enhanced features to the input representation. Deformable sampling provides spatial adaptation to local shape variation, while channel attention adjusts the importance of the extracted responses. Within an MCSS block, MAEM therefore provides morphology-aware local features for the subsequent group-wise state-space transformation, complementing its long-range spatial modeling. 2.4 End-to-End Learning We train the entire network in an end-to-end manner using the Dice loss. Given a predicted segmentation mask Y ^ \hat{Y} and the ground-truth mask Y Y , we minimize ℒ Dice = 1 − 2 ​ ∑ i Y ^ i ​ Y i + ϵ ∑ i Y ^ i + ∑ i Y i + ϵ , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dice}}=1-\frac{2\sum_{i}\hat{Y}_{i}\,Y_{i}+\epsilon}{\sum_{i}\hat{Y}_{i}+\sum_{i}Y_{i}+\epsilon}\,, where the summations run over all pixel locations and ϵ \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 3 Experiments 3.1 Dataset We evaluate our approach on the Synapse Multi-Organ Segmentation dataset [ 7 ] , a publicly available collection of 30 abdominal CT cases comprising 3,779 axial CT slices. We report segmentation performance for eight anatomical structures: the aorta, gallbladder, left kidney, right kidney, liver, pancreas, spleen, and stomach.

3.2 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate segmentation performance using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and the 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95). DSC measures the overlap between predicted and ground-truth segmentations, while HD95 assesses boundary discrepancy. Higher DSC and lower HD95 indicate better performance. 3.3 Implementation Details We trained our model on a GeForce RTX 4090 GPU for 300 epochs. CT slices were resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 , with a batch size of 22 and an initial learning rate of 1 × 10 − 3 1\times 10^{-3} . Quantitative results are reported in Table 1 . MCDNet achieves the highest average DSC of 81.61% among the compared methods, improving upon VM-UNet and MedMamba by 0.53 and 0.94 percentage points, respectively.

Compared with VM-UNet, MCDNet increases the DSC for the pancreas from 58.80% to 63.57% and for the spleen from 89.51% to 90.90%. These results demonstrate the performance of MCDNet across organs with diverse morphologies. Its design combines local morphological adaptation with channel-decoupled long-range modeling. MCDNet achieves an HD95 of 23.72, although several compared methods obtain lower HD95 values. 4 Conclusion We propose MCDNet, a Morphology-Aware Channel-Decoupled Mamba Network for medical image segmentation.

Its MCSS block processes channel groups separately to learn differentiated structural representations and captures long-range spatial context through SS2D. Within each group, MAEM uses deformable sampling and channel attention to adapt local feature extraction to anatomical shape variations. Adaptive channel gating integrates the group outputs, connecting morphology-aware enhancement with channel-decoupled state-space modeling. Experiments on the Synapse abdominal CT dataset demonstrate improved average segmentation accuracy over the compared methods, achieving an average DSC of 81.61%.
